# Proteoforms and drug targeting

::: {.callout-warning}
## First draft
Written from `research/12-proteoforms-drugs.yml` and not yet reviewed by a
second reader. Four of its sources are FDA regulatory documents and one is a
trial registry record, cited as primary evidence for an approval and its trials.
Seven sources are abstract-only, and those carry the proteoform-scale estimate
and two of the historical cases.
:::

A drug binds a molecule with a particular shape, and @sec-what-changes showed
that one gene's isoforms can differ at exactly the surfaces a drug would touch.
If a gene makes several proteins, the practical question is which one is the
target, and whether anything can be aimed at that one alone.

The vocabulary shifts from RNA to protein here. A transcript isoform is an RNA
molecule, while a proteoform is a distinct protein form from one gene. The
second term absorbs differences this book has treated separately: those from
splicing, those from genetic variation, and those added after translation.

## Far more proteoforms estimated than measured {#sec-measuring}

The gap between ambition and measurement is the largest in this book, and two
numbers set its size. A single cell is estimated to carry upwards of a million
different protein forms, built from about 20,000 coding genes
[@proteoformmedicine2026]. A single intact-molecule study reports thousands of
protein forms from a cell lysate [@xu2024topdown]. The estimate counts in
millions and the measurement in thousands.

![Three quantities on one logarithmic axis. The gap between what is estimated to
exist and what one experiment reports is what limits isoform-level drug
discovery. The measured quantity is drawn as a band because the source says only
"thousands".](../figures/proteoform-scale.svg){#fig-proteoform-scale width=100%}

Two styles of mass spectrometry divide the problem. Reading fragments of a
protein gives information about regions of it, while reading the intact molecule
reports which combination of features one molecule actually carries
[@xu2024topdown]. Only the second can confirm that two differences sit on the
same protein.

### Intact molecules, and the window they are read in

The best intact-molecule surveys are larger than the round figure of thousands
suggests, and they are also narrower. A deep survey of two isogenic human
colorectal cancer lines reported 23,622 proteoforms mapping to 2,332 distinct
proteins. That took more than 400 raw files, at a one per cent proteoform-level
false-discovery rate [@mccool2022topdown]. A survey of five human organs
reported 11,466 proteoforms from 740 distinct proteins, of which 8,784 were
unique to a single tissue [@drown2022tissueproteoforms]. Those two counts run in
opposite directions on proteoforms and on proteins, because the first went deep
on two cell lines while the second went wide across organs.

The same authors state the limitation that makes such numbers hard to read as
coverage. Their survey was confined to proteoforms below 30 kDa on the
instrument used, and most of what it identified was 10 kDa or smaller
[@mccool2022topdown]. The reason offered is signal dilution rather than any
property of the protein. A larger molecule spreads its ions across a wider range
of charge states, so its signal-to-noise ratio falls sharply in a complex sample
[@mccool2022topdown].

That ceiling is not absolute, and the exception shows what it depends on. In
single muscle fibres dissected from rats, proteoforms above 200 kDa were
resolved, including myosin heavy chain at about 223 kDa, well enough to classify
each fibre by type [@melby2023singlemuscle]. One sample was a complex human
lysate and the other a single fibre from another species, so the useful reading
is that the window follows sample complexity rather than the technique.

Depth at this resolution is bought with instrument time, and the price has been
reported. Obtaining 13,975 proteoforms from 2,720 proteins in human Caco-2 cells
required 257 separate liquid-chromatography mass-spectrometry runs, about 27
days of net measuring time [@kaulich2024sampleprep]. At matched input the trade
against the peptide workflow is stark. Lysate equivalent to about 250 HeLa cells
gave 2,600 proteins by peptides, and about 250 proteins with about 780
proteoforms by intact molecules [@gao2026topdownbottomup]. Peptides buy protein
coverage, intact molecules buy proteoform identity, and nothing yet buys both.

### Peptides rarely name an isoform

The peptide workflow is the one almost every laboratory runs, and its failure
for isoforms is structural rather than incidental. Three quarters of annotated
human coding genes, 14,698 of 19,449 in RefSeq, carry more than one protein
isoform, and 3,409 carry ten or more [@dou2023sepepquant]. An in-silico tryptic
digest of that database gave 588,545 peptide sequences, 83.5 per cent of them
from multi-isoform genes. About half of those map to every isoform of their
gene, leaving 246,615 that can pin down one isoform or a subset
[@dou2023sepepquant].

Real data are worse than that arithmetic predicts. Across one stem-cell and two
liver-cancer studies, peptides able to discriminate isoforms made up about 35
per cent of multi-isoform peptides and about 27 per cent of all peptides
identified [@dou2023sepepquant]. The shortfall is clearest counted per gene. Of
10,444 genes with any peptide evidence in one human cell type, 5,993, or 57 per
cent, had no isoform that could be confirmed at all. Every peptide found for
them was shared between two or more isoforms [@mehlferber2022huvec].

One further number from that experiment is the one a drug programme needs. Only
106 genes, about one per cent, had two or more isoforms each supported by a
uniquely mapping peptide [@mehlferber2022huvec]. A selective drug has to know
whether the other isoform is also present in the tissue being treated. Direct
evidence that two isoforms of a gene are present at once is almost never
obtained.

The bottleneck is not the one a spectroscopist would predict. Of 969,900 tryptic
peptide precursors generated in silico from the canonical human proteome, only
3,084, or 0.32 per cent, were predicted to be indistinguishable by retention
time and fragmentation pattern on high-resolution instruments
[@elhamraoui2024indistinguishable]. The instruments can tell the peptides apart.
The specific obstacle is abundance, because the peptide that distinguishes one
isoform from another is usually the scarce one and isoforms go unrecorded for
want of signal [@korchak2024isprm].

A named drug target shows how complete that failure can be. A targeted assay
using isotope-labelled whole-protein standards measured about 290,000 Ras copies
per cell in a colorectal line. It returned no signal at all for the
KRAS4A-specific peptide at endogenous levels. Those authors read that as KRAS
being almost entirely KRAS4B in those cells [@mageean2015rasisoform]. The gene
is abundant, the assay was targeted, and one of its two forms was still
invisible.

### Prediction aimed at the instrument

One response is to predict rather than search. Long reads from the same sample
can say which isoform-specific peptides ought to exist, and the instrument is
then pointed at those [@korchak2024isprm]. It works, raising isoform
detectability 3.6-fold over the untargeted approach and finding five isoforms
that no annotation listed [@korchak2024isprm]. The scale bounds what it can be
used for. The experiment confirmed protein for 54 resolved isoforms across 43 of
55 genes, and required a synthetic standard for each of 192 peptides it hoped to
find [@korchak2024isprm]. This is not yet a survey method.

The same move works without targeting, by changing the search database instead
of the instrument. One search replaced reference protein models with
long-read-derived ones, for the 6,653 genes where transcript sampling was
confident. Run against Jurkat spectra, that changed 3,199 protein groups. In 673
of those, 21 per cent, the identification became more specific about which
isoform was present [@miller2022longreadproteogenomics]. Both results point the
same way, and both are the protein-side return on @sec-three-axes.

What the resulting numbers look like for one important gene is sobering. The
first top-down study to cover both KRAS4A and KRAS4B completely characterised 39
proteoforms across colorectal cancer cell lines and primary tumours
[@adams2022krasproteoforms]. Among them was a KRAS4B lacking the C185 residue
and its C-terminal modifications, which failed to reach the plasma membrane and
reduced MAPK pathway activation [@adams2022krasproteoforms]. Proteoform
resolution is not bookkeeping when one entry in the list is a form of the
protein that no longer signals.

Two pieces of infrastructure exist for this, and both describe the distance
still to go. The community programme states its own scale. Assuming 5,000 human
cell types surveyed to a depth of one million proteoforms each, it anticipates
asserting about 50 million unique proteoforms, at a cost target of one dollar
per proteoform [@smith2021proteoformproject]. A machine-readable notation sits
alongside it, introduced in 2018 and extended as ProForma 2.0 so that
modifications at specified or ambiguous positions can be written unambiguously
[@leduc2022proforma]. The second is a prerequisite for the first, because a
catalogue of fifty million ambiguous names would be unusable.

Confidence is itself graded, and the grading is rarely reportable. A proteoform
identification is not a single confident answer, and a five-level system exists
to say how ambiguous one is. Among the top-down search programs tested, only one
reported enough information for that grading to be applied
[@rolfs2021proteoformclass]. A reader of this literature therefore often cannot
tell how firmly a named proteoform was identified.

### Single cells and tissue sections

The RNA side of this book is strongly single-cell and the protein side is almost
entirely bulk. That asymmetry is real, and it is no longer absolute. Proteoform
resolution has reached single-cell throughput without reaching single-cell
depth. About 400 proteoforms were surveyed across more than 17,000 individual
nuclei from human keratinocytes, assigned by matching intact masses to a library
built from bulk runs [@kanchustambham2026snpims]. Spatial measurement sits at a
similar depth. Imaging of human kidney detected about 400 proteoforms below 70
kDa at better than 80-micrometre resolution, and named 169 of them from a
precompiled list of roughly 1,000 candidates [@su2022pims].

Both work by matching against a list made elsewhere, which is the honest answer
to whether single-cell proteoform biology is available. The throughput exists,
the depth does not, and neither study discovers a proteoform it was not already
looking for.

Why this blocks drug discovery in particular has been stated directly. A
candidate cannot be prioritised when it is unknown whether the splicing event
yields a protein, what that protein's structure is, and what it does
[@shaw2022multiomics]. Three therapeutic routes are already in use against
splicing events, which are immunotherapy, oligonucleotides and small molecules
[@shaw2022multiomics]. @sec-cancer-therapeutics and @sec-sma cover examples of
the second and third.

## Claudin-18: a drug that targets one isoform {#sec-isoform-selective}

Claudin-18 settles the question of whether isoform-selective therapy is
possible, because it already exists in the clinic. The licence is dated and its
wording ties the drug to an isoform rather than to a gene. On 18 October 2024 a
United States licence was issued for a claudin-18.2-directed cytolytic antibody.
It covers first-line use with fluoropyrimidine and platinum chemotherapy, in
adults whose HER2-negative gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction tumours are
claudin-18.2 positive on an approved test [@fdavyloyapproval2024].

The two protein forms come from two promoters on one gene, each carrying its own
first exon joined to the same exons 2 to 5 [@claudin18promoters2001]. Promoter
choice rather than exon skipping is what makes the lung form and the stomach
form distinct [@claudin18promoters2001]. One belongs to stomach and the other to
lung [@katoh2026cldn18]. This is the alternative-promoter mechanism of
@sec-what-changes, arriving as a drug target.

![Two first exons, two proteins differing only at one end, and an antibody that
binds the loop present in one of
them.](../figures/cldn18-isoform-target.svg){#fig-cldn18 width=100%}

Selectivity was a design requirement at discovery rather than a property noticed
afterwards. The target-discovery work raised monoclonal antibodies that bind
claudin-18 isoform 2 while not binding the lung-specific variant of the same
gene [@claudin18pancancertarget2008]. That work also reported the narrow
normal-tissue footprint the whole therapeutic argument rests on. In healthy
tissue, isoform 2 appears only in differentiated epithelium of the gastric
mucosa, and not in the gastric stem-cell zone [@claudin18pancancertarget2008].
Avoiding the other isoform was the goal, because the lung form is present in
healthy lung and binding it would do pulmonary harm [@katoh2026cldn18].

The discrimination was then measured rather than assumed, and the regulator's
own pharmacology review records the experiment. Zolbetuximab bound two gastric
cancer lines and isoform-2-transfected HEK-293 cells with dissociation constants
in the low nanomolar range, and did not bind HEK-293 cells transfected with
claudin-18 isoform 1 [@fdavyloyreview2024]. A binding reagent that distinguishes
two products of one gene is what this book has been arguing is possible, and
here it is characterised in a regulatory file.

The trials behind the licence are worth stating with their denominators. In the
larger one, 565 patients were randomised, 283 to antibody plus chemotherapy and
282 to placebo plus chemotherapy. Median progression-free survival was 10.6
against 8.7 months and median overall survival 18.2 against 15.5 months, each
with a hazard ratio of 0.75 [@fdavyloyreview2024]. The second trial used a
different chemotherapy backbone and met its primary endpoint across 507
randomised patients, with median progression-free survival of 8.21 months
against 6.80 and a hazard ratio of 0.687 [@shah2023glow]. Its survival analysis
was reported at an interim point at which 318 of 507 patients had died, 144 of
254 on antibody and 174 of 253 on placebo. Median overall survival was 14.39
against 12.16 months, with a hazard ratio of 0.771 [@shah2023glow].

The isoform selects a large minority of patients rather than a rare subgroup. Of
2,333 patients screened for that trial, status was assessable in 2,104, and 808
of them, 38.4 per cent, met the staining threshold. Among HER2-negative tumours
that rose to 729 of 1,701, or 42.9 per cent [@shah2023glow]. Eligibility is a
staining rule rather than a measurement of the isoform. A tumour qualifies when
at least 75 per cent of its cells show moderate to strong membranous claudin-18
immunohistochemistry. The sponsor justified that cutoff from earlier phase 2
efficacy data rather than from a prospective comparison [@fdavyloyreview2024].

### The companion test cannot see the distinction

The test approved alongside the drug is not itself isoform-selective. Its
antibody was raised against a claudin-18 C-terminal sequence shared by both
protein isoforms, and specificity testing confirmed it detects both
[@fdacldn18cdx2024]. What closes the gap is a statistical argument about
expression rather than a measurement of the right molecule. Isoform 1 messenger
RNA sits near baseline in gastric adenocarcinoma. Where it is detectable,
isoform 2 is higher in 99 per cent of samples, by a median factor of 93
[@fdacldn18cdx2024].

That argument is probably sound, and it is not the same thing as seeing the
isoform. The book's one approved isoform-selective therapy is paired with a
companion diagnostic that cannot resolve the distinction the drug depends on,
and the gap is bridged by the expectation that the other isoform is not there.
It is a measurement gap of exactly the kind @sec-measuring describes, sitting
inside a licensed product.

One more caution belongs with the approval. The two registration trials were not
conducted as planned. The regulator recorded 21 separate unblinding incidents.
In one of them, unblinded treatment assignments sat on a shared site accessible
to blinded staff for about 19 months. It concluded that it could not rule out
bias or data integrity problems [@fdavyloyinspection2024].

### FGFR2b, the same argument with a harder outcome

The companion target is one this book has already met. FGFR2b is the epithelial
form of a receptor whose IIIb and IIIc exons decide which growth factors it
answers to, described in @sec-fgfr. The therapeutic side of it is a true splice
isoform rather than a promoter choice. The IIIb form was reported overexpressed
in roughly 30 per cent of HER2-negative gastric cancers [@wainberg2024fight].
Discrimination between the two splice forms was shown functionally, since cells
engineered to display IIIc were not killed through antibody-dependent cellular
cytotoxicity while cells displaying IIIb were [@xiang2021bemarituzumab].

Isoform selection costs a great deal of screening for a modest trial. Some 910
patients were prescreened to randomise 155. At final analysis the whole
randomised population showed median progression-free survival of 9.5 months
against 7.4, and median overall survival of 19.2 against 13.5, with confidence
intervals crossing one in both cases [@wainberg2024fight]. The benefit tracked
how much of the isoform a tumour displayed. Among patients whose tumours stained
for IIIb in at least a tenth of cells, median progression-free survival was 14.0
against 7.3 months. Median overall survival was 24.7 against 11.1, hazard ratios
of 0.43 and 0.52 [@wainberg2024fight].

Choosing the right isoform did not spare the normal tissue that carries it.
Corneal adverse events affected 51 of 76 patients given the antibody, against 8
of 77 on placebo. They reached grade 3 in 21 patients with none on placebo, and
caused 24 of the 31 discontinuations in the antibody arm [@wainberg2024fight].
One of the two confirmatory phase 3 trials, the one combining the antibody with
a checkpoint inhibitor, was stopped by its sponsor rather than completed
[@nct05111626fortitude102].

How common the isoform is depends on who measured it, by roughly an order of
magnitude. Earlier retrospective series put it near 2.5, 3.7 and 4.9 per cent.
Trial prescreening put it at 29 per cent and then 37.8 per cent. Those authors
attribute the gap to study design, the age of the tissue, the antibody chosen
and the scoring rule [@rha2025fgfr2bprevalence]. The largest estimate comes from
prescreening for the confirmatory trial. Of 3,782 evaluable gastric tumours from
37 countries, 1,428 or 37.8 per cent showed moderate to strong membranous IIIb
staining in any proportion of tumour cells. Requiring at least a tenth of cells
brought that to 612, or 16.2 per cent [@rha2025fgfr2bprevalence].

On the measurement question the two programmes differ in the reader's favour.
The antibody clone used to select patients for the receptor programme is
specific for the IIIb form, whereas the claudin-18 clone recognises both forms
of that gene [@rha2025fgfr2bprevalence]. An isoform-specific companion assay is
therefore achievable, and the approved drug is the one that does not have it.

### CD44v6, the precedent that killed a programme

Picking a splice variant is not by itself a safety argument, and the precedent
is older than either programme above. The larger CD44 proteins arise when
variant exons are spliced into the extracellular part. An antibody raised
against the sequence encoded by variant exon v6 stained the membranes of
squamous cells in the upper layers of skin and tonsil epithelium, in work
published in 1993 [@cd44v6isoforms1993]. An antibody-drug conjugate against the
same variant exon later killed a patient with toxic epidermal necrolysis, after
two infusions at the highest dose reached. The sponsor judged risk-benefit
negative across four phase 1 trials and 70 patients, and stopped development
[@bivatuzumabdoseescalation2006].

Read against the claudin-18 case, the two make a single point. Isoform
selectivity protects a patient only when the isoform's normal-tissue footprint
is narrow, and establishing that footprint is separate work from establishing
the selectivity. Claudin-18.2 had its footprint mapped at discovery. CD44v6 had
its published thirteen years before the fatal trial.

### Most drugs called isoform-selective are not

A reader coming from pharmacology will have met the phrase in a different sense,
and the distinction matters to the argument here. Most agents described as
isoform-selective select between genes rather than between one gene's products.
The class-I phosphoinositide 3-kinases comprise three class-Ia catalytic
subunits and one class-Ib subunit. The one that alpelisib and its research
precursors target is encoded by its own gene, so that selectivity does not bear
on this argument [@jamieson2011p110alpha]. Nothing in this chapter turns on
paralogue selectivity, and the two cases that turn on isoform selectivity are
the two above.

## Resistance by selecting a form already present {#sec-resistance}

Resistance is anticipated to arrive through the same mechanism that created the
target, by the tumour coming to carry an isoform that no longer holds the
epitope [@katoh2026cldn18]. That expectation is reasonable, and the evidence for
it is more complicated than the expectation in a way that changes how it should
be stated.

HER2 is among the most studied targets in oncology, and reading its transcripts
at full length raised its protein-coding isoform count from 13 to 90
[@guardia2025her2]. Much of that diversity had not been recognised before and is
not assessed in routine practice, having surfaced only in a survey of 561
primary breast cancer samples [@guardia2025her2]. Even the two variants already
well known turned out to be families, since nine isoforms lacking exon 16 were
found and only one was in the reference annotation [@guardia2025her2]. Lines
made resistant to the antibody and to antibody-drug conjugates moved their
expression toward isoforms lacking the region the antibody binds, in cell
culture rather than in treated patients [@guardia2025her2].

### CD19, and three readings of one relapse

Cell therapy supplies the best-studied case, and it forces the qualification.
Relapse accompanied by loss of the targeted epitope occurs in 10 to 20 per cent
of children who responded to CD19-directed CAR T cells [@convergence2015cd19].
That is the clinical frequency any molecular account has to explain. Relapse has
been attributed to the tumour changing which isoform of the target it makes
[@barnkob2022carisoform]. An audit of antigens proposed for solid tumours
suggested the problem is general rather than particular to that one target
[@barnkob2022carisoform].

Three findings complicate that account without dismissing it.

The escape form is not manufactured by the therapy. In seventy-five untreated
childhood leukaemia marrows and in healthy blood and spleen, inclusion of CD19
exon 2 had a median near 96 to 97 per cent. A few per cent of transcripts
therefore lack the exon before any drug is given [@dam2026cd19exon2]. In a
re-analysis of four treated children, pre-treatment reads skipping exon 2 were
highest in the patient who relapsed fastest, and absent in the one complete
responder. Four patients support no inference of any kind [@dam2026cd19exon2].
Selection of a pre-existing minor form is the supportable description, and
switching is not.

The protein does not behave as the simple story implies. Expressed in
CD19-deleted leukaemia lines, the exon-2-skipped protein stayed inside the cell
with the endoplasmic reticulum marker calnexin [@bagashev2018cd19er]. The splice
form therefore causes loss of surface antigen rather than a visible receptor the
CAR fails to grip, which is a different mechanism from the one the word
switching suggests.

The genetic explanation may be sufficient on its own. Deep exome sequencing of
paired pre-treatment and relapse leukaemias found a genetic cause in seven of
eight children whose relapse was CD19-negative. Each carried a coding variant
undetectable before infusion, and none of five CD19-positive relapses did
[@chen2022cd19genomic]. In the index patient whose relapse had been attributed
partly to splicing, two frameshift deletions in exon 4 sat at close to half of
reads each. Read phasing put them on opposite chromosomes in 484 of 520 reads
covering both sites. That arrangement would inactivate both gene copies with no
splicing change [@chen2022cd19genomic]. A separate series reported coding
mutations with loss of heterozygosity in nearly all resistant cells, and read
the absence of antigen as irreversible rather than as a reversible shift in
splicing [@geneticmechanisms2018car19].

The splicing reading has not been abandoned, and its defenders argue the genetic
account does not close. One group re-read the same published relapse sample and
noted that the exon 2 frameshift sat at roughly a third of reads, too low to
explain a leukaemia uniformly surface-negative by flow cytometry
[@asnani2019intron2]. That re-analysis also found a different splicing event
dominating. Retention of CD19 intron 2 made up about three fifths of the reads
joining into exon 3 in the relapse sample, and it introduces a premature stop
codon [@asnani2019intron2].

Those sources are less independent than a list of citations suggests. Several
re-sequence or re-analyse the same patients from the same centre, so the
disagreement is partly neighbours arguing over shared samples. What survives is
narrower than the review-level claim. A splice form can contribute to antigen
loss, the dominant mechanism in the one deeply sequenced series was genetic, and
nobody has shown a drug inducing the splice form rather than enriching it.

### BRAF, and whether it is a splicing case at all

The second-best-known case may not belong in this chapter. Shortened BRAF
messages lacking the exons encoding the RAS-binding domain were found in six of
nineteen melanoma patients progressing on vemurafenib. They appeared in none of
twenty-seven tumours from patients never exposed to the drug, and in neither of
two patients with intrinsic resistance [@poulikakos2011braf]. The shorter
protein does not resist because the drug cannot reach it. Vemurafenib inhibited
truncated and full-length kinase at similar concentrations in vitro, and
blocking dimerisation restored sensitivity in cells, so resistance comes from
RAS-independent dimerisation [@poulikakos2011braf].

The splicing attribution rested on a negative result. Array-based copy-number
profiling of the BRAF locus in resistant clones showed no somatic deletion
inside the gene, and patient tumours were not profiled that way
[@poulikakos2011braf]. A mechanism for a splicing cause was supplied later. It
is a single C-to-G substitution fifty-one nucleotides upstream of the intron 8
acceptor, at a predicted branch point, on the mutant allele only
[@salton2015braf].

A 2024 report contradicts the whole account. It attributes the same variants to
genomic deletions, having found matching deletions in melanoma cell models and
in melanoma and breast tumours expressing them. The same report finds the
variants in BRAF wild-type and in untreated melanoma
[@genomicdeletions2024altbraf]. This book does not resolve the disagreement. If
the variants are genomic then BRAF is not an isoform case at all. It is reported
here with its conflict attached rather than used as support.

### Soluble decoys

One recurring route makes the target soluble, so that it leaves the cell surface
and absorbs the drug or the immune signal while the cell goes unharmed
[@choi2025asresistance]. Reviewed across antibody therapy as a whole, the
mechanism recurs on many of the field's principal targets
[@choi2025asresistance].

The primary evidence is strongest for PD-L1. Two splice forms lacking the
transmembrane domain were recovered from the relapsed tumours of two
non-small-cell lung cancer patients who had progressed on anti-PD-L1 antibody.
The same two variants turned up in two of fifteen further refractory patients
[@gong2019spdl1]. How little is needed is the striking part. In mice carrying
engineered colon adenocarcinoma tumours, a mixture in which only one cell in a
hundred expressed the soluble form was already resistant, the rest expressing
normal membrane protein [@gong2019spdl1]. A resistance mechanism that works at
one per cent of cells does not need to sweep a tumour.

Not every anchorless form comes from splicing, which bounds the generalisation.
A second soluble PD-L1 form is thought to arise when transcription terminates
early inside intron 4, upstream of the transmembrane exon. Across thirty-three
tumour types in public data it was most frequent in lymphoma and thymoma, at
roughly a third of cases [@sagawa2022pdl1vint4]. The death receptor FAS has the
same architecture by the splicing route. Forcing a long non-coding RNA that
pairs with Fas pre-messenger RNA in HeLa cells increased skipping of the exon
encoding the transmembrane segment. Soluble Fas rose in the medium, and the
cells were protected from ligand-induced death [@villamizar2016sfas]. A review
states the FAS case in one line [@choi2025asresistance], and the primary
supplies the mechanism and the direction of causation.

### AR-V7, and what a biomarker has to do

@sec-drug-targets presented AR-V7 as the shape of problem where therapy produces
the isoform. The outcome data make the prognostic claim strong and the causal
wording weaker. Among 118 men with castration-resistant prostate cancer starting
abiraterone or enzalutamide, those whose circulating tumour cells carried AR-V7
message did worse on both endpoints. Median progression-free survival was 3.1
against 6.9 months, and median overall survival 10.8 against 27.2 months
[@armstrong2019prophecy]. The response data separate the groups further. No man
positive for AR-V7 protein had a confirmed antigen or tumour response, and 11
per cent of men positive by the message assay did, against 26 to 28 per cent of
negative men [@armstrong2019prophecy].

The marker is specific to a treatment setting rather than general. Among the men
from that study who went on to receive a taxane, AR-V7 status carried no
disadvantage, on a comparison that was descriptive and unpowered
[@armstrong2020taxane]. A single-centre cohort of 65 men dissents on the marker
itself. A third of AR-V7-positive men, 11 of 33, still had an antigen response,
against 20 of 32 negative men. The amount of message did not differ between
responders and non-responders, and AR-V7 status carried no independent
prognostic weight [@schlack2022arv7]. A prospective blinded multicentre study
and a single-centre cohort disagree, and the first is the better design.

One group turned the problem round into a selection rule worth repeating, which
is to aim at the isoforms a tumour gains rather than at the ones it can afford
to lose [@barnkob2022carisoform]. Isoform switching under drug pressure is
better described as isoform selection, and on current evidence it is one
mechanism among several rather than the general form of acquired resistance.

## Reagents that discriminate between proteoforms {#sec-modalities}

If a target is an isoform, the binding reagent has to discriminate at that
resolution. Two approaches are being developed, and both run into the same
circular problem.

Single-domain antibodies keep full binding capacity at one-tenth the size of a
conventional antibody [@vanfossen2025nanobodies]. The property that matters here
is discrimination rather than affinity, since they can distinguish shapes of the
same protein that differ only slightly [@vanfossen2025nanobodies]. RPS24 showed
in @sec-rps24 that reagents of this selectivity can be made for a difference of
three residues, and zolbetuximab shows the same for a difference at one protein
end.

Raising a reagent against one protein form requires having that form in quantity
and purity first [@vanfossen2025nanobodies], so measurement and reagent
development are each waiting on the other.

Targeted degradation inherits the same blind spot in a more dangerous form. A
degrader designed against a protein does not distinguish that protein's forms,
so it may remove the harmless one and leave the harmful one to take over
[@cui2026proteoformdegradation]. Stated the other way round, a drug aimed at a
gene's canonical product may work against some of that gene's protein forms and
not others. The result is adverse effects, or a failure to achieve what was
expected [@cui2026proteoformdegradation]. A proteoform-blind drug need not fail
outright to be failing part of the time.

## Proteoform medicine as a programme {#sec-programme}

The position now being argued is that protein forms sit between genotype and
phenotype rather than alongside them [@proteoformmedicine2026]. On that account
they are the layer at which disease mechanism and drug action actually operate.

Two technologies are named as making the programme feasible, and one of them is
the long-read sequencing of @sec-three-axes [@proteoformmedicine2026]. The claim
is framed as a dependency rather than an aspiration. Treatment at this
resolution requires measurement at this resolution [@proteoformmedicine2026].

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The review is here as an abstract only

The review is in this corpus as an abstract, so only its abstract-level
statements are cited. Its account of the network biology, its treatment of
specific diseases, and any figure in it have not been read. The primary behind
its million-proteoform estimate is not in the corpus either, so that figure
reaches this book secondhand. Readers who want the argument in full should go to
the paper rather than to this section.
:::

## Where this leaves the argument

The position has four parts and they do not resolve into one verdict.

Isoform-selective therapy already works in the clinic. An approved drug draws
its selectivity from which first exon a gene uses, the discrimination is
characterised in a regulatory file, and the design deliberately spared the other
isoform to avoid harming healthy tissue. A second programme, against a true
splice isoform, reached phase 3 with a stronger effect in the isoform-high
subgroup than in the trial as a whole.

Selecting the right isoform is not the same as being safe, and the record
includes a death. CD44v6's presence in normal skin was published more than a
decade before an antibody-drug conjugate against it proved fatal. The receptor
programme produced corneal events in two thirds of treated patients, and one of
its confirmatory trials was stopped by its sponsor. Isoform selectivity bounds
the tissue a drug can harm, and only the normal-tissue map says where that bound
lies.

Resistance through isoform identity is real and narrower than it is usually
stated. The evidence supports a drug selecting a form the tumour was already
making rather than a tumour switching on demand. For CD19 the dominant mechanism
in the one deeply sequenced series was genetic rather than a splicing change,
and the best-known second case may be genomic rather than post-transcriptional.
What survives is a mechanism with good primary evidence in soluble PD-L1 and
FAS, and a selection rule that follows from it.

The measurement is still not adequate to the ambition. Confirming that a
particular protein form is present in a particular tissue, in enough copies,
with its epitope intact, remains a targeted experiment rather than a survey.
About one per cent of genes have two isoforms each confirmed by a unique
peptide. That it matters anyway is shown by a licensed drug depending on a
distinction its own companion test cannot make, with the gap covered by an
argument about expression rather than by seeing the molecule.
